author: Andrew Davis
title: John Newman stepping down as head of VIM Hilton Head Island - NewsBreak
text:
By Andrew Davis ,
5 hours ago
HILTON HEAD ISLAND, S.C. (WSAV) – John Newman came to Volunteers in Medicine (VIM) of Hilton Head Island in 2020 to continue to build on the charitable organization’s tradition of health care for all.
Now, six years later, he is stepping aside from the organization for a different calling. It’s something he called a dream in more ways than one.
“It’s always at two in the morning,” Newman said. “Then something’s waking me up and it’s like, ‘I need you to do something.’ I don’t know why the Lord does this to us, but he finds a way to make us uncomfortable. And you think about, ‘What do you want from me?'”
That’s when Newman received a phone call.
“I got a call from the U.S. Navy that was like, ‘Would you consider coming back?'” Newman said. “Because we would appreciate your gray hair. I was like, ‘Let me think about it.’ And I spent a lot of time and thought and prayer, and I don’t think I could find a more disruptive thing to do for my life or my family. But just as soon as I said, ‘Yep, I’ll do it.’ You know what? Since then I’ve been sleeping like a baby.”
Newman has been in the Navy before as a surgeon. He was in private practice before coming to VIM.
He called the job he stepped into six years ago a big challenge and incredibly rewarding.
“When I got here, I thought the challenge was, ‘All right, how do we deliver the best health care for the patients in our community?'” said Newman. “And then I realized with some guidance from some of the folks around here, this is, you know, maybe that’s not totally your job here. And so, my challenge is really how to find and get the most out of retirees and volunteers and to make it to where they feel like they have purpose and they have commitment.”
Newman said he quickly found that getting the most out of these hard-working volunteers was not difficult to do. Their work ethic delighted him.
“You’ve got people that volunteered in this clinic for 30 years, and I’m just like in awe of these doctors, these nurses, and lay volunteers. But they wouldn’t do it if they didn’t feel like they got something out of it,” said Newman. “And at the end of the day, they get more than they get, which is kind of, I think, the secret of life.”
He continued, “I fell back in love with medicine. I could just walk to this clinic. And behind every door there’s a volunteer and a nurse and provider who’s caring for somebody. And I just knew that was the joy in me. And so just falling back in love with, you know, a mistress that, you know, had changed a little bit over the years, but is like now she she’s still here and is still warm, is the warmest of all hearts. When you walk around those halls as we’re teaching our students the joy of medicine and, you know, when you measure your days on the number of hugs you get, that’s a pretty good way to measure the quality of your day.”
Newman says he also learned this community loves and supports VIM, and cares deeply about the people who need its services.
“I think the people that get it, the people that love help know that everything about it when you drive on this island, and you just feel it, you smell the platform and you feel a community like this. They also know who’s doing the work to keep our resorts open to friends and family, to keep our restaurants open to us, to keep our golf courses, our landscapers, our housekeepers, the people that are doing that work, they’re working their tails off, said Newman. “But most of them don’t have access to health insurance, and volunteers and medicine provide that for them because we want them to be happy in their work. We want them to continue with the beautification and the joy of Hilton Head Island. But they need help from us to keep them because illness is real.”
Some of Newman’s help is coming from an expanded wellness program with hydroponics that are growing heads of lettuce, collard greens, fruit trees and plants in the parking lot that he planted himself.
“I accidentally am growing over a thousand heads of lettuce a week with the hydroponics,” said Newman. “I accidentally got a couple of hundred fruit trees scattered around a parking lot. And it’s amazing just watching them grow up. That’s where wellness is, is gaining this momentum. But that momentum paired with illness is just amazing. So, when I look at the future of Volunteers in Medicine, I mean, I’m thinking thousands and thousands of square feet that need to go for wellness. They’re going to be seeing as many people in the wellness prevention side as we’ll be seeing them on the illness side. And that’s sometimes that’s 200 patients a day we’re seeing in the clinic. But wellness is already up to thousands a year, thousands.”
Newman is leaving the clinic in better shape than he found it, but he said he has one regret from his time on Hilton Head Island.
“Shame on me for not working on this six years ago, but one of the key things we did is we legislated this special volunteer license, which allowed somebody with a medical license from anywhere in the country to come and practice with a special volunteer license,” said Newman. “But our nurses don’t have that. Our physical therapists don’t have that. Our occupational therapists don’t have that. So, if they want to practice in them, they actually have to obtain a South Carolina physical therapy, occupational therapy, nursing license. And for those who don’t want to go through that stuff, I think that impedes some of the volunteerism that we could have. I would seriously consider finding ways to legislate a special volunteer license for these people that aren’t going to be able to practice without that type of license.”
He also offered a few words of advice to his staff, or anyone who cares about VIM and its patients.
“If there’s a new doctor or a nurse on this island, they haven’t been here a week, somebody bug them,” said John. “Hey, you need to go over to them and help out VIM.”
Newman’s last day at VIM will be in September.
He is headed to Japan and then most likely to a field hospital in the East to help train the next generation of surgeons and to help his new set of patients, the military men and women fighting for our country.
But Newman said no matter where he goes, VIM holds a special place in his heart. The next time he is on Hilton Head Island will be as a volunteer doctor himself.
“The last two words of our mission statement are to touch their lives with love and in the process heal ourselves,” said Newman. “I think we’re doing that. Thank you for keeping Volunteers in Medicine deep in your heart.”
